text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure for this public goods game: keeping tokens privately gives me 1 point each but costs others 0.75 per token, while contributing to the group account gives everyone 0.75 points per token including me. I'm setting up the formula for my total payoff based on how many tokens I keep versus contribute.

Working through all the scenarios confirms it: keeping dominates regardless of what others do (15 vs -30 if I give while others keep, 65 vs 20 if I keep while others give), even though mutual cooperation yields the best group outcome. Since this is a one-shot decision embedded in a repeated 10-round game, a purely rational choice points to keeping everything, though I recognize this sacrifices the higher collective payoff that cooperation would produce.

reply.thinking:
I'm working through the payoff structure: each member starts with 20 tokens, where keeping a token privately nets +1 for self but costs each of the other three members 0.75, while putting a token in the group account only gives the contributor 0.75 back with no effect on others.

So comparing outcomes: full cooperation (everyone contributes everything) yields 15 points each, while full defection (everyone keeps everything) yields -25 each once the externalities stack up, even though keeping is individually dominant since 1 > 0.75 from a self-interested view ignoring spillovers.

Since this repeats over 10 rounds, it's a classic social dilemma where cooperation is collectively better despite the individual incentive to defect. For the first round, I'll start by contributing fully to the group to signal cooperative intent and see how others respond -- if everyone matches that, we'd each net 60 overall.

Summing across all members, each own-kept token nets -1.25 socially (1 to self minus 0.75 to each of three others), while each group token nets +3 socially, showing group contribution is collectively optimal even though individually keeping tokens pays more per token to oneself.

Comparing full cooperation versus full defection: if everyone contributes all 20 tokens, each ends with 60+45=105 points, but if everyone keeps everything, each ends with only -25+45=20 points — a classic social dilemma where individual incentive to defect undermines the collectively superior outcome.

Given it's repeated over 10 rounds, I'll start by contributing the full 20 tokens to the group fund to signal cooperation and see how others respond.
